query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: During rapid thermal processing of noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles, there exists an optimal narrow time window at the target synthesis temperature in which limited atomic mobility enables a disorder‐to‐order transformation while simultaneously kinetically trapping the multielement mixture into a single-phase solid solution. Deviating from this window (e.g. by prolonging the heating pulse) allows sufficient surface diffusion for species with lower diffusion activation barriers to segregate and form secondary phases or intermetallic clusters.
generation.material_initial_state: Disordered, solid-solution HEA nanoparticles (~4–5 nm) synthesized by rapid (ms-scale) heating from metal salt precursors, with homogeneously mixed noble and non‐noble elements.
generation.intervention: Control the duration of a post‐initial heating step at a fixed temperature (e.g. 1100 K), by systematically increasing the annealing time (e.g. from 5 minutes to 10 minutes) while maintaining the rapid cooling rate.
generation.conditions: Processing under rapid heating/cooling conditions and a controlled, short additional heating period at around 1100 K; applicable in regimes where kinetic trapping is essential (e.g. Joule-heated or plasma‐synthesized systems).
generation.structural_mediator: The extent of atomic ordering measured via XRD (e.g. appearance of intermetallic superlattice peaks) and STEM-ADF mapping showing elemental distributions, as well as particle size uniformity assessed by TEM.
generation.mechanism: The short re-heating pulse provides just enough thermal energy to lower the Gibbs free energy (ΔG) of a more ordered configuration without affording extensive atomic diffusion. In the multi-element (noble metal–dominated) system, the effective dilution of each species (resulting in reduced local concentration) and relatively high activation barriers for some species help suppress extensive elemental migration. However, if the heating time is too long, atoms with lower surface diffusion barriers (or with intrinsically weaker bonding) have time to segregate, leading to phase separation, elemental segregation, and growth or alteration of the crystal structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Within the optimal heating duration, nanoparticles will transition from a disordered HEA to an ordered, single-phase solid-solution structure while maintaining a small, uniform particle size. Extending the heating duration beyond the optimal window will result in detectable phase separation (e.g. appearance of intermetallic phases or elemental clusters), increased particle growth, and non-uniform morphology.
generation.baseline: The previously reported synthesis using a rapid initial Joule-heating step followed by a ~5 min reheating at 1100 K with rapid cooling yielding stable, single-phase MPEI nanoparticles.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to noble metal–based HEAs with more than five elements processed under rapid thermal regimes where both high heating rates (ms to s) and controlled short-duration annealing are possible. It may not hold for systems where the initial elemental diffusion is uncontrolled (e.g. solution-based syntheses) or for compositions with drastically different elemental diffusivities beyond those typical in noble-metal intermetallic compounds.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from the disorder-to-order transition study (PMC8797181::web::003::introduction) supports controlled heating as key to obtaining the ordered phase, and kinetic models (PMC10621632::web::022::simulated_particle_formation_and_influen) suggest that limited diffusion is essential, it remains uncertain how subtle variations in individual surface diffusion activation energies among noble versus non-noble components quantitatively affect segregation in different noble metal-based HEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several batches of noble-metal based HEA nanoparticles under identical initial conditions and then vary only the duration of the reheating step at 1100 K (e.g., 5, 7, 10 minutes) while maintaining rapid cooling. Characterize the crystal structure and elemental distribution of each batch using XRD, high-resolution TEM/STEM, and elemental mapping.
measurements: XRD for phase purity and detection of superlattice peaks indicating ordering or phase separation
TEM/STEM for particle size, morphology, and crystallinity
EDS mapping to detect any elemental segregation within particles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If extending the reheating duration beyond the nominal optimal period does not induce any measurable phase separation, increased particle growth, or altered ordering (i.e. the structural characteristics remain identical to the 5-min sample), then the hypothesis that limited thermal exposure is critical for kinetic trapping and phase selection would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The combined data analyses from XRD and XAS evidence clearly that the elements in the five-metal precursor reduce stepwise. However, a single-phase alloy forms nonetheless. This behavior contrasts with the bimetallic case, suggesting that the rules governing phase formation differ for the systems containing two or five elements: Single-phase alloy formation occurs more readily if more elements are present, as systems that are immiscible on the bimetallic level can be driven to mix by introducing more elements. As the resulting phases of the binary particles cannot readily be explained by their thermodynamic stability, we devised a kinetic model to rationalize the experimental results based on the restrictions imposed by the synthesis. When comparing five-element and two-element mixtures, the concentration of individual atom types is reduced the more elements are present. This will make it increasingly difficult for elements with strong preferences of ordering to form an intermetallic structure or for elements that repulse each other to segregate, simply because they are more dilute. In this work, we demonstrate the synthesis of nanoscale MPEIs (4 to 5 nm) that contain up to eight different elements without particle growth or phase separation via a unique multi-elemental disorder-to-order (HEA to MPEI) phase transition strategy (Fig. 1A). Specifically, we first rapidly Joule-heated metal salt precursors on the carbon substrate [x-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy characterization in fig. S2] at ~1100 K for 55 ms to produce disordered solid-solution HEA nanoparticles as the starting material (). We then use the precise heating control made possible by this Joule-heating approach (in which the reaction temperature is controlled by an electric current) to reheat the HEA nanoparticles for just 5 min at ~1100 K to promote atomic rearrangement to a more thermodynamically stable MPEI configuration (i.e., a disorder-to-order transition), followed by rapid cooling to lock the final ordered structure in place. The resulting MPEI nanoparticles feature an intermetallic structure that has two sublattices (A1B1) (fig. S3a).
